title: Why the Whiteman band looked like an advancement
summary: The large Whiteman orchestra, with Grofe, Jimmy Dorsey, Chester Hazlett and a film planned, appealed to the young arranger.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Jazz musicians on film and studio scoring

blocks.x: I was elated and for an arranger, a guy who had just been arranging for a year, here was a band with strings yet. Four, only four of them, but that's they way they used them then. Then he had four trumpets, four trombones. He had eight saxophones, and he was playing theatres and he was playing 1812 Overture and all that junk but all these guys had jobs. Oh, the picture, he had a movie picture in mind. They were going to make a moving picture.
That's the one that came out in 1930.
The King of Jazz, so this to me

looked very solid and besides there was a guy, Ferdie Grofé, who -- I had never met him, but I was always a great admirer of his music ability, his arranging, and then there was Jimmy. He said, "You ought to come with us," and Tommy was in the band then and Red Nichols had left, had been in the band and left and there was some talk of Miff, but I understand that Miff never got to the band. At that time.

And they had, what, here's a guy with a sub-tone, Chester Hazlett and they had so many things that you could use and good musical surroundings, Malneck, and they had a saxophone player, Max Farley and then they had the Rhythm Boys, which didn't particularly appeal to me. You know, I didn't know them -- they also had another trio that they used to use quite a bit. They had six singers, so as far as I was concerned, I was looking forward to September and the end of the job.
